content.text: {"relation":"REFINED","consensus_summary":"Across all three blind responses the consensus core is: a disciple is a committed learner-follower of Jesus who continues in his word, imitates him, obeys him, and bears fruit; in mainstream usage the term is functionally equivalent to 'Christian' (Acts 11:26) and describes every believer, with secondary senses covering the Twelve, generic adherents of any teacher, and the disciples as literary representatives of the church.","book_summary":"The book identifies the disciple as one in whom the law is sealed (Isa 8:16) — the new-covenant law written within (Jer 31:33) — proven by continuing in the word, love, and fruit, and conditioned on the three 'cannot' statements of Luke 14 (leaving one's own, bearing the cross, forsaking all). Baptized into the Name, the disciple is perfected 'as his master,' the One in whom the Name, covenant, and law dwell, with the Name-in-forehead imagery of Rev 14:1 attached.","consensus_core_identification":"Disciple = committed follower/learner of Jesus; in dominant Christian usage coextensive with 'believer'/'Christian.'","book_core_identification":"Disciple = a follower of Jesus in whom the law is covenantally sealed/written, defined by meeting the Luke 14 conditions (forsaking all, cross-bearing) and bearing the Name — i.e., a conditioned, proven status rather than a designation for every believer.","core_relation":"BOOK_NARROWS","extension_relation":"BOOK_SUBSET","boundary_disagreement":"The consensus (and the book's own common-view note) treats 'disciple' as any believer, entered by faith and baptism. The book restricts the term by conditions: those who will not leave their own, bear the cross, and forsake all 'cannot' be disciples, and true disciples are those in whom the law is sealed. This excludes believers who have not met these costly conditions, making disciples a proven subset of believers rather than the whole class. This resembles Response A's minority 'two-tier believer/disciple' alternative and edges toward Response B's rare 'advanced class' reading.","material_contradiction":"None at the level of central referent: the book still identifies the disciple as a follower of Jesus continuing in his word (John 8:31), which is the consensus core. The disagreement is over conditions and extension, plus a distinctive covenantal-Name framing (Isa 8:16 + Jer 31:33 + Ex 23:21 + Rev 14:1) that adds symbolic content the consensus does not carry but does not deny the follower-learner identification.","rationale":"The book preserves the consensus's general category — a follower of Jesus proven by continuing in the word, love, and fruit (John 8:31; 13:35; 15:8 territory) — so this is not DIVERGENT. But it materially tightens the boundary: it foregrounds the Luke 14 'cannot' conditions as constitutive rather than hortatory, and redefines the disciple through Isa 8:16 as one in whom the law is sealed, linked to the new-covenant heart-writing and the Name written in the forehead (Rev 14:1's 144,000). This shifts 'disciple' from a synonym for 'Christian' to a conditioned, sealed subset, which is a real boundary disagreement with the majority view while remaining within its category — the definition of REFINED. The reading is also anticipated as a minority/rare alternative in the blind responses, confirming it is a recognized narrowing rather than a novel referent.","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"One could argue MATCH: the book's proof marks (continuing in the word, love, fruit) and cost passages are exactly the consensus's own primary basis, and Luke 14's conditions are quoted by all consensus responses; the 'law sealed' language could be read as merely a covenantal description of every believer (Jer 31:33 applies to the whole covenant people), in which case the book's extension would be identical to the consensus's. The counter is that the book's framing — conditions that make some professing followers 'cannot' be disciples, plus the Rev 14:1 sealed-Name linkage — signals a proven, restricted class distinct from 'any believer,' which the book's own common-view note is set against.","confidence":"high"}
